title: Saudi Arabia downs three Houthi missiles over Riyadh, second attack in three days
dek: The Saudi-led coalition said it intercepted the ballistic missiles after its strikes on Houthi targets in Sanaa and Hodeidah. An Indian was killed in a Houthi strike on Riyadh's airport in October.
author: Declaration Desk
body:
Saudi air defences shot down three ballistic missiles fired by Yemen's Houthi movement towards Riyadh early on Saturday, the Saudi-led coalition said, in the second attack on the Saudi capital in three days. Explosions were heard over the city after residents received emergency alerts on their phones, according to reports.

The coalition's spokesman, Major General Turki Al-Maliki, announced the interceptions on X shortly after 2 am Saudi time (4.30 am IST). "Air defences intercepted and destroyed (3) ballistic missiles launched by the terrorist Houthi militia toward Riyadh," the coalition said. Saudi Civil Defence, which had issued an "aerial threat" alert at 1.53 am, later lifted it, saying the danger had passed. No casualties had been reported.

## What happened

The Houthis said on X that they were striking targets across Saudi Arabia, including Riyadh. Early-warning alerts were also issued in Al-Sulayyil, south of the capital, in Najran near the Yemeni border, and in Jazan and Khamis Mushayt in the south-west, according to reports.

On Friday evening two ballistic missiles aimed at Jazan were intercepted, and debris fell in the Al-Shuqaiq area, according to reports. Over the whole of Friday the coalition reported intercepting five drones and three ballistic missiles.

On Thursday a Houthi strike damaged several floors of a tower in Riyadh's King Abdullah Financial District and neighbouring buildings; Civil Defence reported no injuries. Saudi Arabia's foreign ministry condemned attacks on civilian and economic facilities, said they threatened regional and international security, and said the kingdom reserved the right to defend its sovereignty, according to reports.

## The coalition's strikes in Yemen

Saturday's missiles followed what the coalition called a "special operation" on Friday against targets in Yemen. It said it struck a main Houthi supply depot in Sanaa and was carrying out operations against Houthi missile capabilities in Sanaa, Saada and Taiz and against facilities at the Red Sea port of Hodeidah. The coalition said the aim was to remove threats to civilians in Yemen and Saudi Arabia. The Houthis had threatened reprisals for those strikes. The Houthis' own account of damage and casualties from the coalition strikes could not be independently confirmed.

## Background

Saudi Arabia leads a military coalition that backs Yemen's internationally recognised government against the Houthis, who control Sanaa and much of the country's north. A truce that had largely held for about four years ended earlier this year, when the Houthis resumed attacks on Yemeni government forces and on targets inside Saudi Arabia, according to reports.

The fighting is part of a wider period of conflict in the Gulf. Earlier this month the Houthis claimed strikes on Saudi oil routes, and shipping in and around the Strait of Hormuz has been hit by mines and projectiles, as The Declaration has reported.

## Why it matters for India

Saudi Arabia is home to one of the largest communities of Indian workers abroad and is one of India's main suppliers of crude oil. A Houthi strike on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport on 10 October killed an Indian national and injured several others, according to reports.

After that attack the Indian Embassy in Riyadh told Indian nationals to take shelter immediately when emergency alerts are issued, move to interior rooms away from windows, avoid crowded places, follow Saudi official announcements rather than unverified reports, and not film or share pictures of security incidents. It said the emergency number is 911 in the Makkah, Madinah, Riyadh and Eastern Province regions and 998 elsewhere. The embassy had not issued a fresh advisory after Saturday's attack by the time of publication.

## What happens next

The Houthis have warned airlines to avoid Saudi airspace and have threatened Saudi Red Sea ports, according to reports. Neither side has signalled any move towards a renewed truce.
